title: Making karah prashad
hook: equal parts flour, sugar and butter, cooked while reciting

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhog: a full reading of the Granth brought to its close with the last pages, the Anand and Ardas. Your line was end well. What did you finish yesterday with a little more care than usual? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-two.

Flour, sugar, butter. Three ingredients sitting on a counter, and nothing about them looks holy. Then the flour goes into a heavy pan with the melted butter and someone starts to stir. It darkens slowly, from pale to gold to the color of an old coin, and the kitchen fills with a warm, toasted smell. Sugar dissolved in water goes in with a hiss. And all the while, the person at the stove is saying something under their breath, not a shopping list, not a song from the radio. Words of the Guru. At the end of a gurdwara service, this is what lands in people's hands. Today the Sikh code tells us how it is made.
screen: `FLOUR, SUGAR, BUTTER.` → `STIRRED UNTIL GOLDEN.` → `WORDS UNDER THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Karah is the deep iron pan, and prashad is a gift given by grace. So karah prashad is grace from the pan. The Sikh Rehat Maryada gives the recipe in paraphrase: equal parts of wheat flour, sugar and clarified butter, prepared in a clean vessel by someone who has bathed, reciting Gurbani while it cooks. Start with the measure. Equal parts. No ingredient is the star. That is easy to remember, and it asks for nothing a plain kitchen doesn't already have. Next, the cook. The code doesn't ask for a priest. It asks for clean hands, a clean pot and a mind on the Guru's words. The prayer isn't added at the end like a garnish. It is stirred in the whole time. Then the bowl comes into the congregation. The code describes stanzas of the Anand being recited and Ardas offered, and the prashad touched with a kirpan before it is shared. Last, the sharing. The code says it is given to everyone in the sangat alike, without asking about caste. Whoever you are, you hold out your hands, and the same sweet warm handful lands in them as in everyone else's. Some families make it at home too. It's the same recipe, and the same rule: pray while cooking. A kitchen becomes a place of remembrance, and an ordinary chore becomes a way to hold the Guru's words for as long as the pan is on the fire.
screen: `KARAH PRASHAD: GRACE FROM THE PAN.` · `EQUAL PARTS, A CLEAN VESSEL.` · `RECITED WHILE IT COOKS.` · `SHARED WITH EVERYONE ALIKE.` · then, large: `PRAY WHILE COOKING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cook something while praying. Right now, settle and choose what it will be. A pot of rice tonight, a cup of tea in an hour, toast in the morning. Something small. Then choose the words you'll keep under your breath while you make it. If you pray, it might be a line of Gurbani you know, or simply Waheguru. If not, it might be the names of the people who will eat it. Sit with your hands open in your lap, the way people hold them out for prashad, and rehearse it once in your mind: the pan, the stirring, the words. The bell holds the time.
Making karah prashad. Equal parts flour, sugar and clarified butter, made with clean hands while reciting Gurbani, then shared with everyone alike. Today's word.
Your line: pray while cooking. Today, the next time you make anything to eat, keep a few words going under your breath until it's done. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, karah prashad is prepared from equal parts flour, sugar and ghee while Gurbani is recited, presented with Ardas, and handed to everyone in the congregation in cupped hands.
